s1-001-e08743dadfaf0f0f.wav.text: Last time we fixed the stride and got fifteen times.

s1-002-353c11168f512bd5.wav.text: Today we fix the volume, add threads, add a register tile, and then spend the last third of the episode being honest about the seven times that remains between us and OpenBLAS.

s1-003-74eef576cbfb85cb.wav.text: That last part matters more than the optimisations, because knowing where a gap lives is a transferable skill and a tuned constant is not.

s2-001-6ad6f0b1f06cbf12.wav.text: Here is the second problem, which is a completely different one.

s2-002-aa501d04e192d3b5.wav.text: The i k j loop touches memory in the right pattern, and it still streams the entire B matrix past the cache once for every single row of A.

s2-004-a996acad43d3d962.wav.text: At n equals one thousand and twenty four, in double precision, B is eight megabytes.

s2-005-500f0e5ebe6c5a1e.wav.text: That fits in no cache on this machine.

s2-006-dd566696e602daca.wav.text: One row of A consumes all of B, and there are one thousand and twenty four rows.

s2-007-a382d267c8a8b0bf.wav.text: So the kernel moves something on the order of eight gigabytes of traffic to perform two gigaflops of arithmetic.

s2-008-c55f371e9d2d5f6e.wav.text: Remember the arithmetic intensity from last episode.

s2-009-d94f3e0a223c6f01.wav.text: Eighty five flops per byte available.

s2-010-558e1dfcbd5e1278.wav.text: We are collecting about a quarter of one.

s2-011-927e7490083e40ea.wav.text: Stride is about how you use a cache line once you have it.

s2-012-cd1c7c3efb0d6690.wav.text: Volume is about how many times you go and get the same data.

s3-000-4e289c9c132711be.wav.text: The fix is blocking, and the picture is simple.

s3-001-34009b7631d28b03.wav.text: Instead of streaming all of B for each row of A, take a panel of B.

s3-002-4759c8e84ed9b856.wav.text: Sized so that it fits in the cache level you are aiming at.

s3-004-f799c94e1502948f.wav.text: Then push many rows of A through that resident panel before you let it go.

s3-005-9c0ff7a824986cac.wav.text: The traffic drops by roughly the number of rows you reuse it for.

s3-006-121cf1afee2bf69f.wav.text: In this implementation there are three block sizes.

s3-007-d09a36972419c838.wav.text: M C, how many rows of A per tile.

s3-008-4ce9e6884e9c0e2c.wav.text: K C and N C, the two dimensions of the B panel.

s3-009-4a23d8ff24c68cb7.wav.text: The defaults aim the B panel at a quarter of a megabyte, which is roughly L2 on this machine.

s3-010-ddba9f3f0325b800.wav.text: And the crucial word in that sentence is roughly, which the next scene is about.

s4-000-5684cb785e7712ab.wav.text: Now, everyone expects a block size sweep to reveal a magic number.

s4-001-990d857b15e9417b.wav.text: Here is the actual sweep, six plausible tilings at n equals one thousand and twenty four.

s4-002-0b623963a2960af1.wav.text: The best is one twenty eight, one twenty eight, two fifty six, giving thirteen point five five.

s4-003-9de876b3245733b2.wav.text: The worst is sixty four, two fifty six, one thousand and twenty four, giving ten point five three, and that one is worst because its B panel is two megabytes and no longer fits.

s4-004-91f49716bdd417ea.wav.text: Worst over best across the whole table is one point two seven times.

s4-005-19e84100f76c4d6c.wav.text: That is the finding, and it is more useful than a magic number would have been.

s4-006-309ec37bbc474ef0.wav.text: Block size is not a constant you tune to three significant figures.

s4-007-0aa621e4251b5115.wav.text: It is the sentence, make the panel roughly L2 sized.

s4-008-3a8823d1a2f0a20d.wav.text: Anything in that neighbourhood is within twenty percent, and the twenty percent is not where your remaining seven times is hiding.

s5-000-d122853f3c9cedf2.wav.text: And here is how you find that neighbourhood without reading a spec sheet.

s5-001-00af3340d9f38ae1.wav.text: Take an array, scale it in place, and time it.

s5-002-4dfce46097f35221.wav.text: Two bytes move per array byte, one read and one write.

s5-004-5070ca6ac8a5ecab.wav.text: At sixteen kilobytes we get forty one gigabytes per second, and that row understates because the per call overhead is a real fraction of the time.

s5-005-d06bb060f5cc2a47.wav.text: At two hundred and fifty six kilobytes, seventy one.

s5-006-3c7add2fdf933d11.wav.text: At one megabyte, eighty one, the peak.

s5-007-0841f1bcfe2c526c.wav.text: And then at four megabytes it falls off a cliff to forty four, and by sixty four megabytes it is down to thirty four, which is main memory.

s5-008-9a9e60b2b87a36de.wav.text: Read the cliffs, not the absolute numbers.

s5-009-14be7d8ddac17c51.wav.text: The cliff between one and four megabytes is a cache level ending, and it is precisely why the sweep preferred a panel of a quarter of a megabyte.

s5-010-aa1b207b65973041.wav.text: This chart took nine lines of NumPy and it is worth more than any spec sheet, because it describes the machine you are actually running on today.

s6-000-d0439fb6b81cbed2.wav.text: Threads next, and the interesting part is choosing which loop to parallelise.

s6-001-0f9ae9ebe8828f63.wav.text: We parallelise over j j, the column tiles.

s6-002-37b30650a8a42bf2.wav.text: Each thread owns a disjoint band of columns of C.

s6-003-a13e37d087282807.wav.text: Disjoint writes mean no locks, no atomics, and no reduction step at the end.

s6-004-9ba00149cbb52187.wav.text: Compare that with parallelising over k, which would have every thread accumulating into the same elements of C, and would need either atomics or per thread buffers and a merge.

s6-005-00a03033896f5361.wav.text: Same arithmetic, dramatically different engineering, decided entirely by which index you hand to OpenMP.

s6-006-433e7e8dd9a1fead.wav.text: And notice the restrict keyword on the two pointers.

s6-007-ecf28f79e5e5ecf9.wav.text: That is a promise to the compiler that these arrays do not overlap.

s6-008-d4c6f6d462c941f8.wav.text: Without it the compiler must assume that writing to C might change B, which forbids hoisting the value of A out of the inner loop and forbids vectorising the store.

s6-009-574c10e3739356fa.wav.text: One keyword, and a large fraction of the optimisation.

s7-000-3f296ca9d78429a4.wav.text: Threading gets us from a hundred and eighty one milliseconds to a hundred and twenty five.

s7-001-361e756f2bf54d62.wav.text: One point four five times on two cores, not two times, and I want to name that rather than quietly move past it.

s7-002-c9944f01731787ad.wav.text: The kernel is partly memory bound, and the two cores share a single memory system, so adding a core adds arithmetic capacity and adds no bandwidth.

s7-003-5e05279af4e1c7b1.wav.text: Sub linear scaling on a memory heavy kernel is the expected outcome.

s7-004-2b10dd1932ce10a9.wav.text: If you ever see linear scaling on a kernel like this, that is the surprising result and it usually means you were more compute bound than you thought.

s7-005-ab1296d8e9b92f7a.wav.text: Adding a four row register tile takes us to a hundred and fifteen milliseconds and eighteen point seven gigaflops, which is where our hand written ladder ends.

s8-000-15ce414a25eb93b9.wav.text: And now the part I think is worth the most.

s8-001-548e68b1997871fc.wav.text: We are at eighteen point seven, OpenBLAS is at one hundred and thirty five, and the honest question is where the difference goes.

s8-002-fdfa525925b1c1fa.wav.text: None of it is C being slow.

s8-004-1032efd613060b1b.wav.text: Our kernel does not hold C in registers.

s8-005-ba14fdc0fb00a8a4.wav.text: Every fused multiply add carries a load of C and a store back to C.

s8-006-2c9d2b9015fe13c5.wav.text: A real micro kernel holds a small tile of C, say eight by six doubles, entirely in vector registers, accumulates across the whole k loop, and stores it exactly once at the end.

s8-008-74412333a0fbf5fb.wav.text: BLIS style kernels copy the A and B panels into contiguous pre swizzled buffers, so the micro kernel sees perfectly aligned unit stride data with no page table pressure.

s8-009-11b8324630396419.wav.text: Third, hand written assembly, per micro architecture, software pipelined, with explicit prefetch instructions.

s8-010-1c217a53cdfae963.wav.text: And the reason the first one matters most to you is that it is precisely what the GPU pass in phase seven calls accumulating in registers.

s9-001-004a65991a9c0658.wav.text: Stride and volume are different bugs.

s9-002-b3a3693c1e1479ff.wav.text: Loop order fixes one, blocking fixes the other, and confusing them wastes a lot of time.

s9-003-891c9ac77fc5adc5.wav.text: Block size is roughly L2 sized, the sweep is flat within one point two seven times, so stop tuning it and go find a real bottleneck.

s9-004-e7731af9808ba156.wav.text: Measure your own memory hierarchy in nine lines of NumPy and read the cliffs rather than the absolute numbers.

s9-005-cafc86d47e663c3d.wav.text: Parallelise over whichever index makes the outputs disjoint, and you will need no synchronisation whatsoever.

s9-007-a1a6ca46af033a7d.wav.text: Twenty two point six times from blocking alone, thirty five point six with threads and a register tile, landing at fourteen percent of this machine's theoretical peak for reasons you can now list on demand.

s9-008-13c3ce2d67ec1576.wav.text: Phase seven rebuilds this entire chain of reasoning on a GPU, where shared memory plays the part of L2 and the sentences do not change.

s9-009-c6869a084c0ca224.wav.text: Next topic is forty five A.
